title: AWS Introduces Native Vector Search for DynamoDB
gist: Amazon DynamoDB has shipped native vector search — a new index type with a SearchVectors API supporting up to 4096 dimensions, inline filtering and three distance functions — letting developers store embeddings beside application data and drop the separate vector database and its sync pipeline entirely. AWS pitches trillions-of-vectors scale at single-digit millisecond latency, while practitioners debate whether AWS is late and whether per-byte index billing makes it pricier than S3 vector buckets.

themes.theme: Collapsing the standalone vector database out of the stack

insights.claim: Amazon DynamoDB now supports native vector search, letting developers store embeddings alongside application data and run approximate nearest-neighbor queries without operating a separate vector database.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: The bundling of vector search into a mainstream managed OLTP database directly attacks the standalone vector-DB category's core value proposition.
insights.locator: Amazon DynamoDB recently introduced native vector search

insights.claim: Before this release, applications on DynamoDB had to copy data into a separate vector database and keep the two systems synchronized, adding architectural complexity and data transfer that native vector search now eliminates.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Removing the sync pipeline is the concrete switching incentive; incumbent vector DBs relying on being the second system in an AWS stack lose the integration tax they were being paid to solve.
insights.quote: increasing architectural complexity and data transfer
insights.locator: Until now, applications using the managed NoSQL database

insights.claim: DynamoDB vector search is model-agnostic on embeddings, explicitly supporting Amazon Bedrock Titan Text Embeddings, Cohere Embed and OpenAI text embedding models.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: AWS is not gating the storage layer to its own embedding models — embedding APIs stay a competitive, substitutable commodity while the durable lock-in sits in the database.
insights.locator: Developers can choose any embedding model

insights.claim: DynamoDB vector indexes support up to 4096 dimensions, Euclidean, Cosine and Dot product distance functions, and inline filtering, with no stated storage limits and horizontal scaling as data grows.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: 4096 dimensions covers essentially all current commercial embedding models, so dimension ceilings are no longer a reason to pick a specialist vector store.
insights.quote: It supports up to 4096 dimensions, Euclidean, Cosine, and Dot product distance functions, and inline filtering.
insights.locator: DynamoDB is fully serverless, so vector search scales automatically

insights.claim: AWS VP and chief evangelist Jeff Barr claims DynamoDB vector search scales to trillions of vectors while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: If the trillions-of-vectors-at-single-digit-ms claim holds in production, the technical case for specialist vector infrastructure narrows to features and cost rather than scale.
insights.quote: This scales as big as you want it (think trillions of vectors) while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.
insights.locator: Jeff Barr, VP and chief evangelist at AWS, highlights on LinkedIn

insights.claim: AWS positions DynamoDB native vector search at agentic memory, retrieval augmented generation, recommendation engines, personalized experiences and anomaly detection as the target workloads.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Agentic memory being named first in AWS's own workload list shows hyperscalers now treating agent state as a mainstream database use case, not a niche.
insights.quote: You can now build applications that require semantic retrieval on agentic memory, retrieval augmented generation, recommendation engines, personalized experiences, anomaly detection, and more
insights.locator: Vector indexes have no storage limits and scale horizontally

themes.theme: Cost mechanics and the S3 comparison

insights.claim: DynamoDB vector indexes are billed on three separate dimensions on top of standard table charges — data written into the index, data processed when searching, and data stored — all metered per byte and billed per GB.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Search-time metering means cost scales with query volume, not just corpus size — a materially different unit economics profile from provisioned vector clusters and a real budgeting risk for high-QPS agents.
insights.quote: You pay for the data you write into the index, the data processed when you search, and the data you store. All three are metered per byte and billed per GB.
insights.locator: They explain the cost implications of the new feature

insights.claim: AWS's own solutions architects name four levers for cutting vector search cost on DynamoDB: lower embedding dimensions, minimal index projections, excluding embeddings from query results, and selective partitioning.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: That AWS leads with cost-reduction guidance at launch implies naive implementations get expensive fast — a checklist for anyone modeling AI application infrastructure spend.
insights.locator: According to the authors, using lower dimensions

insights.claim: A community commenter argues that while DynamoDB will scale well with very low latency, it will probably be considerably more expensive than S3 vector buckets, which offer limitless scale and consistent if unimpressive latency.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: AWS now competes with itself on vector storage; the latency-versus-cost split between DynamoDB and S3 vector buckets is the tiering decision buyers will actually make.
insights.quote: S3 has limitless scale and will provide a consistent latency, even if the latency isn't great. I think DynamoDB will generally scale out pretty well too, with very low latency, but will probably be a lot more expensive than S3.

insights.claim: Some practitioners argue AWS is too late to the party on vector search given that many databases have already shipped vector support over the last couple of years, though the feature drew mostly positive community reception.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Late-but-bundled is historically how AWS erodes specialist categories; lateness matters less than default placement in existing DynamoDB deployments.
insights.quote: some practitioners argue that AWS is "too late to the party."
insights.locator: With many databases having already shipped vector support

insights.claim: Developers are still unclear whether DynamoDB applies attribute filters before or after the vector search runs, an unresolved semantics question with direct implications for recall and cost.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Pre- versus post-filter behavior is the classic differentiator between vector engines; ambiguity here is where specialist vendors will aim their competitive messaging.
insights.locator: Some developers wonder whether DynamoDB applies attribute filters

insights.claim: AWS plans to ship vector search through ExtendDB, its DynamoDB-compatible adapter, for local development and self-managed deployments, and vector indexes are already available in every region where DynamoDB runs on Standard or Standard-IA table classes.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Day-one global region coverage plus a local-dev path removes the usual adoption friction, accelerating displacement of bolt-on vector stores.
insights.locator: The team plans to ship vector search through the DynamoDB-compatible adapter ExtendDB
